item.research_question: Can a high entropy alloy of transition metals absorb significantly higher amounts of hydrogen than its constituent elements, potentially reaching an H/M ratio greater than 2 without using rare-earth elements?
item.processing_route: Arc-melting stoichiometric amounts of Ti, V, Zr, Nb, and Hf (99.6-99.995% purity) five times with re-melting and turning over; sample re-melted with Ti getter to minimize oxygen; hydrogenation performed on ball-milled powder (<50 μm) at 20 bar H2 and 400 °C for 48 h.
item.test_conditions: Gravimetric measurements at 400 °C; volumetric PCT measurements at 299 °C (±1) with pressure up to ~50 bar and 10 h equilibrium time per point; Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS) with 5 °C/min heating ramp.
key_findings: The as-synthesized TiVZrNbHf alloy crystallizes in a single-phase BCC-type structure with a unit cell parameter a = 3.3659(2) Å.
After hydrogenation at 400 °C for 48 h, the alloy forms a body-centred tetragonal (BCT) lattice with a = 3.2183(4) Å and c = 4.6556(16) Å.
Gravimetric measurements yielded a hydrogen-to-metal ratio (H/M) of 2.42.
Volumetric PCT measurements showed a maximum storage capacity of 2.5 H/M at 53 bar H2, equivalent to 2.7 wt% hydrogen.
Hydrogen desorption occurs in a one-step reaction with onset as low as 200 °C and a maximum pressure peak above 400 °C.
The hydrogen absorption/desorption process is reversible, regaining the BCC-type structure after desorption.
XRD patterns after desorption show doublets indicating phase separation into two different BCC phases with slightly different unit cell parameters.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the large hydrogen storage capacity is due to lattice strain caused by the variation in atomic radii of the constituent elements (δ = 6.82%), which makes it energetically favourable for hydrogen to occupy both tetrahedral and octahedral interstitial sites, a configuration not typically accessible in pure transition metal hydrides.
item.limitations: The observed H/M ratio of 2.5 corresponds to only about 2.7 wt% H due to the high mass of Hf and Zr; a neutron diffraction study was not possible due to the large neutron absorption cross-section of Hf; detailed investigation of structural stability during cycling is outside the scope of this communication.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that much higher storage capacity by weight percent can be achieved by replacing heavy elements like Hf and Zr with lighter ones; theoretical modelling using ab initio methods is needed to explain the influence of strain on hydride stability; in situ hydrogenation details are currently being evaluated.
quotes: large hydrogen-storage capacity is due to the lattice strain in the alloy that makes it favourable to absorb hydrogen in both tetrahedral and octahedral interstitial sites
